name: Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control
intent: Hand an object the collaborators it needs instead of letting it build or look them up itself, so that its needs are visible, it can be tested with fakes, and the choice of real parts is made in one place.
scenario: An order service charges a card, sends an email and reads the clock. It is written four ways: it builds the real parts itself, it takes them in its constructor, it asks a global service locator for them, and it takes nine collaborators wired by a container. A test then runs a checkout against each design with fakes, again with one fake forgotten (the mailer), and a fourth dependency is added with 4 existing tests.
problem: Code that creates or looks up its own collaborators is hard to test and hard to read. A checkout that builds a real payment gateway charges a real card in every test, and nothing in its signature tells a reader that it also sends email and reads the clock. Dependency injection moves the choice of collaborators out of the class and into whoever builds it. The traps are on both sides: a service locator hides the needs again behind a global, and a container with every class injected through an interface turns a three-line wiring into nine parameters, a configuration language, and behaviour nobody can follow by reading the code.

howItWorks.title: Separate using a thing from choosing it
howItWorks.text: Inversion of control is the broad idea that your code does not drive everything: a framework or a caller supplies the pieces and calls you. Dependency injection is one form: an object receives its collaborators instead of constructing them. The order service says what it needs (a gateway, a mailer, a clock) and something else decides which real or fake ones it gets. That something is the composition root, usually the program's entry point.

howItWorks.title: Prefer constructor injection
howItWorks.text: With constructor injection the needs are the constructor parameters: a reader sees three dependencies, and the object cannot exist half-built. A test that forgets the mailer fake fails at once, before anything runs: 0 real effects reached. The alternatives are setter or property injection, which allows a half-built object, and passing a dependency to the one method that needs it, which is good when only that method uses it.

howItWorks.title: Beware the global in disguise
howItWorks.text: A service locator is a global registry the class asks for what it needs: Located.checkout() calls the registry. Tests can still replace parts, but the constructor reveals nothing, so a test that registers two of three fakes runs and sends 1 real email without any warning. A static singleton or a new inside the method is the same problem with fewer steps: the test of one checkout reaches 3 real effects and cannot replace any of them. Practitioners disagree about locators: some use them inside frameworks and at the edges, and most agree that using them throughout domain code hides what a class needs.

howItWorks.title: Let a container do the wiring, not the thinking
howItWorks.text: A DI container builds the object graph from registrations, usually by matching constructor parameter types, and manages lifetimes (one instance for the whole program, one per request, or a new one each time). That removes boilerplate in a large program. It also moves behaviour out of the code: which implementation is chosen, and for how long it lives, is decided by configuration that you cannot read in the class. A short-lived object captured by a long-lived one is a classic bug that no compiler sees.

howItWorks.title: Inject what varies, not everything
howItWorks.text: Inject the things that reach outside the process, that are slow or non-deterministic, or that a test needs to replace: a gateway, a mailer, a clock. Pure helpers such as a string formatter or a rounding function can just be called. When all nine collaborators are injected through an interface with a single implementation, a fourth dependency touches 8 files instead of 6 and the tests need 9 fakes to say what they could say with 3.

pros: Tests replace slow, external or non-deterministic parts with fakes, so they run fast and reach no real systems
A constructor lists what the class needs, which is documentation that the compiler keeps honest
Swapping an implementation (a different payment gateway, an in-memory store) is a change in one composition root
Missing wiring shows up early, at construction time, instead of in the middle of a request
cons: More parameters, interfaces and wiring code to read and keep in step
A container hides the object graph and the lifetimes in configuration, which moves some errors to run time
Constructors that take many parameters are a sign of a class doing too much, and injection makes that visible rather than fixing it
Interfaces created only to allow a fake can be noise when there is one implementation and no test needs a replacement
whenToUse: Collaborators that reach outside the process: databases, payment gateways, email, queues, HTTP clients, the clock and random numbers
Code that needs unit tests without real infrastructure
Applications with more than one implementation to choose between by environment or configuration
Libraries and frameworks that call your code (a plug-in point, a handler), where inversion of control is the whole design
whenNotToUse: Pure helpers and value objects: calling a function or creating a small object directly is simpler and just as testable
Small scripts and one-off tools, where a hard-coded dependency is clear and short
As a reason to add an interface and a registration for every class; inject what varies or must be replaced
A service locator in domain code, where it hides what each class needs; keep it, if at all, at the edges of a framework
pitfalls: Creating the real collaborator with new inside the class, or reading a global singleton, so every test reaches the real gateway and cannot replace it
A service locator in the middle of domain code: the constructor says nothing, and a test with one missing registration runs against the real thing
Injecting everything through an interface with one implementation, so a simple class needs nine parameters and a test needs nine fakes

Treating the container's magic as design: when two implementations of a type are registered, some containers quietly pick one (often the last registration) where others refuse to start, and nobody can say which one runs without reading the configuration
Lifetime mistakes: a long-lived singleton holding a short-lived or per-request dependency keeps one stale instance for the whole program
Constructors with six or more parameters accepted as normal: that is usually a class with too many jobs, and a container only hides it
Passing the container itself into classes so they can resolve what they need: that is a service locator with extra steps

roles.label: Order service
roles.description: Charges, emails and stamps the time; needs three collaborators.

roles.label: Composition root
roles.description: The one place that chooses real or fake parts and builds the service.

roles.label: Service locator
roles.description: A global registry the service asks for its parts.

roles.label: DI container
roles.description: Builds the object graph from registrations and lifetimes.

roles.label: Real systems
roles.description: The card gateway, the mail server and the clock.

quiz.question: An OrderService constructor takes a gateway, a mailer and a clock. A test builds it with a fake gateway and a fake clock and forgets the mailer. With constructor injection, what happens?
options: The test runs and sends one real email.
The checkout charges the card first, then fails at the mail step.
The test is skipped, because the service cannot tell what is missing.
The service cannot be built, so the mistake shows before anything runs.
quiz.explanation: A constructor makes every need mandatory: the object does not exist until all of them are supplied. A service locator is the design where the same mistake runs silently against the real mailer.

quiz.question: What is the clearest difference between constructor injection and a service locator for the same class?
options: A locator is faster, because it avoids passing parameters at all.
The constructor shows what the class needs; the locator hides it behind a global.
A locator cannot be used in tests, because the registry is read-only.
Constructor injection needs a container, while a locator never needs one.
quiz.explanation: With a locator the class asks a global for what it wants, so the signature reveals nothing and a missing registration is found at run time. Both approaches can be tested and neither needs a container.

quiz.question: A team injects every class, nine collaborators per service, each through an interface with one implementation. What does the simulation show it costs?
options: Fewer files to edit when a dependency is added, as the container wires it.
Nothing, as long as the container validates the wiring at startup.
More fakes in every test and more files per new dependency, for little gain.
A faster test suite, since every collaborator is replaced by a fake.
quiz.explanation: Nine fakes per test and 8 files for a fourth dependency, against 3 fakes and 6 files with constructor injection of only what varies. Six of the nine are trivial helpers a test never replaces.
